South Korea: USSR Won't Discuss Sakhalin Koreans with Japan is declassified CIA document 0000102975, dated May 1, 1983. The sample is a Korea Herald report, carried in English in June 1983. It quotes Prime Minister Yasuhiro Nakasone on the Soviet refusal to treat returning Koreans as a topic for talks with Japan.

Since 1975, the Soviet Union had allowed only three Koreans to leave Sakhalin for Japan, the report says. Japan was willing to accept all 438 Koreans who had applied for entry permits there. cia-0000106275: Communist Road Development in Laos is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000106275, dated November 4, 1965. The heading tracks road building by communist forces inside Laos. cia-0000108475: Weekly Situation Report on International Terrorism - 23 July 1980 is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000108475, dated May 1, 1980. cia-0000119675: Untitled CIA record from February 1969 holding a statement by John Sweeney. Nothing in the heading says who Sweeney was or why his words were taken down. cia-0000124275: Dated November 1957, this CIA item notes the announcement of the earth satellite launching at a Soviet embassy reception, the date in the heading breaking off. Moscow unveiled its triumph to diplomats in a social setting. The item captures that rollout as the agency heard of it. Embassy receptions doubled as listening posts in the Cold War, and a launch announced over drinks became a reportable event for every service watching that room.
cia-0000126875: From August 1968, a CIA report gathers reaction across the Third World to the Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia. Newly free nations had just watched a superpower crush a smaller state. The paper collects their responses, which ran from anger to silence to cold calculation. Third World answers were tallied because the invasion landed in the middle of the contest for the new nations, whose votes and ports both blocs wanted.
cia-0000126975: An October 1975 CIA Weekly Review covers Angola under the heading After Independence. Formal independence was a month away, and civil war among the rival movements was already under way. The review looks at what came next as Portugal prepared to leave. The review's timing is its irony. Independence day fell on November 11 that year, and the after in its heading already meant a country at war with itself.
cia-0000132275: Situation Report 581 belongs to the CIA's Iraq-Kuwait series. Dated January 1, 1991, it covers political developments. cia-0000132575: A boundary dispute between Peru and Ecuador fills a CIA document dated October 1, 1960. The headline shortens Peru to Pru, a slip kept from the original. cia-0000132675: Rebel work growing inside Cuba fills a CIA paper dated March 4, 1961. Its headline misspells activity as activitty, a slip kept from the original. un-ga-res-a-69-75: Young diplomats learn the trade of disarmament through a UN training plan backed in Resolution A/69/75, from the Assembly's sixty-ninth session. un-ga-res-52-175:
Guatemala's peace moved into its next phase under Resolution 52/175, passed by the General Assembly in 1998. The UN Verification Mission in Guatemala had its mandate stretched to 31 March 1998 by a vote of March 1997. A July 1997 text had urged all sides to push ahead with the second phase of the peace plan, which ran to the end of that year.

The text weighs the mission's seventh report on human rights. It also weighs a report on the strides made by Central American lands in peace, freedom, and growth. The Secretary-General's counsel on the mission's work is before the Assembly: how to shape it so it can meet the needs of the peace check in full.
un-sc-res-75: Who pays for the helpers of UN field teams? Security Council Resolution 75, passed on 27 September 1949, takes up that small but real cost. A 1948 Assembly vote had left it to the Council to rule if a team member needs a deputy at his side. Where that need is found, the UN may pay back the travel and daily costs of such deputies, for time past as well. The text lists the teams whose members had each needed such help, from the Good Offices team in Indonesia on.
un-sc-res-1375: The official series of Council decisions runs through Resolution 1375, catalogued here for 2001. cia-0000139475: A third 1986 report from the DCI's hostage location task force is preserved as document 0000139475. The task force existed because Americans were being seized and held in Beirut and elsewhere, and finding them fell in part to intelligence work. frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d75: Roosevelt wrote to Secretary Hull on October 30, 1943, as the secretary prepared to leave Moscow. The letter is Document 75 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The Moscow agreements had to be turned into summit plans at once, and the president's letters that day pushed the work along. The catalog record names the two men and the date. The letter is part of the Foreign Relations series' Moscow closing papers.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d175: A further letter from Roosevelt to Hull is dated October 30, 1943, and it stands as Document 175 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d275:
A secret memorandum of conversation at Cairo on 26 November 1943 records a meeting about air supply to China over the Hump, the air route across the Himalayas. It is signed by Generals Arnold, Stilwell, and Somervell, and it answers a demand from Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek.

Chiang wanted a fixed 10,000 tons a month flown in, whatever Southeast Asia operations might need. The generals explain that all C-46 aircraft are assigned to the route. They add that 25 more planes are sought for Mountbatten. Mountbatten's lower figure of 8,900 tons differs from the target by only 1,100 tons, which better efficiency may erase. Chiang closes by accepting the figures, with the understanding that the Air Transport Command will strain to raise the tonnage beyond the target.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d375:
Minutes kept by Major John Boettiger record the dinner at Tehran on 30 November 1943, at half past eight in the evening, given for Churchill's sixty-ninth birthday. Thirty-three members of the three delegations sat down together, with Roosevelt on the host's right and Stalin on his left, and a seating plan is attached.

All the speeches took the form of toasts, in the Russian custom set the night before. Roosevelt opened by proposing the toast to the King, a privilege he had asked as an old friend of George VI. Churchill praised Roosevelt as a defender of the weak and toasted Stalin as worthy of the name Stalin the Great. Stalin answered that the honors belonged to the Russian people, and that in Russia even cowards became heroes, while those who did not were killed. Boettiger notes a shared sense that a historic understanding, and lasting friendships, had been reached.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d475:
President Roosevelt sent a second message to Marshal Stalin on December 3, 1943, as the follow-up to the Tehran Conference continued. Roosevelt was by then at Cairo, preparing for the second conference there with Churchill. The State Department preserved the message in the Cairo-Tehran volume, alongside the day's other traffic.

Paired cables to the same leader on one day usually mean fast-moving business, and early December 1943 gave the alliance plenty of it. Roosevelt's exchanges with Stalin in this period set the tone for cooperation in the war's decisive year. Readers get the alliance's most sensitive channel, running at full speed just after its first summit.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d575:
Dean Acheson, Acting Secretary of State, recorded this memorandum on September 7, 1945. Acheson was minding the department while Secretary Byrnes attended the foreign ministers' meeting in London. The memorandum appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

Acheson would become one of the chief builders of the postwar order, and his acting-secretary papers show that order being improvised in its first week of peace. The London meeting was already exposing cracks among the wartime allies. For readers, the memorandum offers a front-row record from the moment the wartime coalition began turning into the Cold War's opposing camps.
frus-1944-quebec-d75:
Officials on the Working Security Committee prepared a memorandum dated August 30, 1944. The committee dealt with security questions in wartime planning. Its paper appears among the pre-conference records in the Quebec 1944 volume. The State Department published the volume after the war.

Committee papers like this one turned broad concerns into staff work. Planners weighed security needs as the war moved toward Germany. Their conclusions fed the briefings prepared for Quebec. For readers, the memorandum shows the middle layer of government at work. Specialists framed questions that cabinet officers and leaders would later decide.
frus-1944-quebec-d175:
At their afternoon meeting on September 12, 1944, the Combined Chiefs took up coordination with the Soviet Union. Sir Alan Brooke said he felt Stalin's offer should be dropped: missions already existed in Moscow, and the Russians need only appoint a suitable senior officer. Portal warned that exchange missions with field commanders would leak plans and gain nothing. The British recommendations were approved.

Zones of occupation in Germany proved harder. The chiefs agreed the question carried such serious political weight that they could recommend nothing without guidance from their governments. Britain wanted the northwest zone on military grounds. King suggested America could take the southwest if its troops could be supplied through north German ports. The chiefs decided to ask Roosevelt and Churchill for an early decision.
frus-1944-quebec-d275:
General Ismay sent Leahy a draft passage on September 15, 1944, built on an idea General Marshall had raised at that morning's meeting. The Combined Chiefs, the draft says, desired to record the Quebec Conference's main difficulty. It had been finding room and opportunity to deploy against Japan the massive forces every nation concerned was ardent to engage.

In colloquial language, the draft continues, it was a case of "standing room only," even before the curtain rang up. The chiefs made no recommendation on the subject in their final report. But including the thought in the communiqué, and at the closing press conference, would hearten world opinion and depress Japan. A draft communiqué filed with the letter matches the one actually issued.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d75:
Who would be invited to found the United Nations? Acting Secretary Stettinius put that question to the President on 15 November 1944. His memorandum, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, is titled “Invitations to the Conference and Initial Membership.” It records a sharp split with Moscow.

Two issues are set out. First, should only the thirty-five United Nations signatories be invited, or also nine associated nations from earlier conferences? Second, should the sixteen Soviet republics enter as original members, as Moscow demanded? The American position was to invite forty-four nations and refuse the sixteen republics. The British and Chinese stood with Washington on the invitations question.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d175:
Washington told King Peter, through Ambassador Patterson, what it thought of the Tito–Subasic plan. The State Department's memorandum to the British Embassy of 23 December 1944 is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. Eden had suggested the step in a telegram to Halifax five days earlier.

Patterson is cleared to tell the King that the Department has studied the papers with attention. Their principles, taken as a whole, match those the United States holds in its own dealings. But so much turns on the goodwill and cooperation of the men named to run the new government that Washington will not judge the plan's chances. Whether it works in loyal practice, the memorandum implies, only the men themselves can show.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d275:
No linkage: that is the order Stettinius sent Harriman on 3 January 1945 about prisoners. His secret cable, number 18, is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It answers the news that Soviet negotiators had been named for General Deane.

In any talks on repatriation, the Department is extremely anxious that two streams be kept apart. Americans found in German camps are one matter. Soviet nationals found among the German prisoners taken by American forces are another. Trouble has already arisen over who counts as a Soviet national. A few men taken fighting with the Germans bear Slavic names but disclaim Soviet nationality. Over eleven hundred Soviet nationals found in German ranks were handed to the Soviet authorities at a west coast port the week before.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d375:
Hiss took notes as Molotov answered the American report on Dumbarton Oaks at the plenary of February 7, 1945. The Soviet side, Molotov said, was satisfied with Stettinius's report. Certain questions had become much clearer after the explanations. Churchill's remarks had also drawn close Soviet attention.

The outcome, Molotov judged, would secure the unity of the three powers in guarding peace after the war. The Soviet aim all along, he said, was the greatest unity among the three on peace and security. The proposals, with the President's changes, would win cooperation from nations great and small. Hiss's shorthand catches Moscow warming to the world body.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d475:
London news fills these excerpts from Grew's cable of February 4, 1945. Winant had told the Soviet member of the European Advisory Commission of American acceptance, in principle, of five French proposals. They concerned French participation in the surrender, occupation, and control of Germany. The Soviet member thanked him for the advance notice and sought early instructions from Moscow.

Winant had also informed the Soviet and British members of American approval of the protocol on German zones. Further down, the cable turns to the Associated Nations. Medina in Venezuela, it notes, was somewhat taken aback by the President's letter, but appreciated the situation. The digest mixes summit questions with embassy detail.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d75:
President Truman accepted Stalin's proposed start date for the Allied move into their German zones on June 18, 1945. His top secret telegram, number 297, is document 75 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Stalin had said mine clearing in Berlin would run to late June, and asked that the pullback begin July 1 instead of June 21.

Truman says he has ordered the American commanders to begin the movement on July 1, as Stalin asked. He assumes American troops will reach Berlin earlier, in enough strength to do their work preparing for the conference. A long editorial note explains the swap of messages behind the decision. The exchange fixed the ground on which the Potsdam meeting itself would stand.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d175:
The British Chiefs of Staff answered the last American points on the staff agenda in a memorandum dated June 29, 1945. The paper, C.C.S. 880/5, is document 175 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It replies to the U.S. memorandum of June 27 on the coming Anglo-American staff talks.

The British say their paper on command against Japan will include plans to reorganize command in the Southwest Pacific. They agree to put off discussion of Russian participation until after the talks with the Russians end. Papers will be swapped in advance where possible. But the British doubt they can ready their papers more than a few days before Terminal. Those papers cover their own role against Japan and command questions. Volume two of Ganguli's Mahabharata brings the Pandavas out of exile to claim their rights. Krishna himself carries their peace terms to the Kaurava court, speaks with courtesy, and is refused with contempt. Both sides then muster armies drawn from half the kings of India.

On the field of Kurukshetra the slaughter begins. The Bhagavad Gita sounds at the battle's heart, as Krishna steadies Arjuna for the fight. Days of duels and massed charges follow, with famous warriors falling in turn. Ganguli's Victorian prose keeps the huge action clear. The peace has failed; the epic's terrible center has begun.
tob-13329-15475:
Books four to seven, in volume two of Ganguli's Mahabharata, carry the Pandavas from hiding back to open war. A year in disguise at a foreign court ends in revelation and alliance. Krishna's peace mission to the Kauravas fails against pride and envy.

Then Kurukshetra's eighteen days begin in earnest. The Bhagavad Gita stands at the center, Krishna's teaching to a warrior who cannot bear to fight his kin. Armies clash, vows are kept at terrible price, and heroes fall daily. Ganguli's prose rises to the scale of the fighting. The epic's blazing middle is all here.
lee-octopus-devil-fish-1875:
The octopus got its first fair trial in Henry Lee's monograph of 1875. The Octopus; or, The Devil-Fish of Fiction and of Fact splits the real beast from the kraken of tale. Lee wrote from his work at the Brighton Aquarium, where he kept the creatures live.

He tells what the octopus is, how it feeds and moves, and how big it truly grows. Then he shows how its arms and bulk swelled, in sailor talk, into a ship-sinking fiend. The book shrinks the legend down to the animal, and the animal stays strange enough. It is the first scientific word on its theme.
rockefeller-commission-report-1975:
A presidential panel judged the CIA's acts at home in June 1975 and found much to blame. The Rockefeller Commission report tells of mail opened, of the CHAOS files on war foes, and of MKULTRA drug tests. Nelson Rockefeller chaired the panel for President Ford.

The report prints the facts of the abuse and the laws it broke, in the government's own words. One part, on the killing of foreign chiefs, was cut by the White House before the book came out. The gap is noted in the file and in the lore of the age. The volume marks the first great public reckoning with the agency.
olcott-people-from-the-other-world-1875:
Henry Steel Olcott went to a farm in Vermont to test claims of ghosts in 1875. The farm was the home of the Eddy kin, whose dark room drew crowds. Olcott, then a news man, watched, weighed, and took notes with a cool head and an open mind.

People from the Other World tells what he found there. That trek changed his life. Soon past it he helped found a new creed with Blavatsky. The book is the start point of that creed's tale, writ by a man on the spot. Olcott had served as a law hand and a war sleuth in his past. Those trades taught him to weigh proof with care and calm.
sargent-proof-palpable-immortality-1875:
Epes Sargent claims the dead can be touched in The Proof Palpable of Immortality, his book of 1875. Forms that took shape in the dark room are his theme. Hands were grasped, faces seen, and weights and prints taken by fans who swore the forms were not the seer in dress or mask.

Sargent prints their sworn tales in dense rows. He holds such proof ends all doubt on life past death. Foes found fraud in case past case since then. The book is the high tide mark of that strange wave of faith.
kardec-spirits-book-1875:
Allan Kardec built a faith from talks with the dead in The Spirits' Book, here in English from 1875. Kardec was a school man in Paris who put the same asks to seers in town past town. Their replies, he held, agreed. The book sets those asks and replies in ranks: God, souls, birth past death, and the laws of right and wrong.

His faith, called Spiritism, claims to join science and creed as one. It won hosts of fans, most of all in Brazil. The book is its first and chief text. All its lore starts here.
rink-tales-traditions-eskimo-1875:
Hinrich Rink spent years in Greenland as a Danish official, and this set of tales came out in 1875. He gathered the tales from Inuit tellers in their own land. The book brought Greenland's oral lore to English readers on a large scale for the first time. Rink had the tales writ down in the tongue in which they were told.

The tales tell of hunts, spirits, ghosts, and the deeds of old heroes. Many show the angakok, the shaman, at work between men and hidden powers. Rink kept the voice of the tellers close, so the book reads as Greenland speaking for itself.
thomas-erceldoune-prophecies-murray-1875:
Thomas of Erceldoune, called Thomas the Rhymer, was a Scots seer and poet of the 13th century. James A. H. Murray edited his romance and forecasts for the Early English Text Society in 1875. The text gives the old Scots words with full notes.

The romance tells how Thomas met the Queen of Elfland and got the gift of true speech. The forecasts that bear his name deal with kings, wars, and the fate of Scotland. Murray's edition is the full record of a lore that Scots quoted for ages. The old Scots text is given with care and full gloss.
lartet-christy-reliquiae-aquitanicae-187:
Edouard Lartet, a French digger, and Henry Christy, an English backer, dug the caves of the Dordogne from 1865 to 1875. Thomas Rupert Jones put their great memoir in print in 1875. Its Latin title means relics of Aquitaine, the old name of that part of France.

The book sets out carved bone, stone tools, and the frames of Cro-Magnon man from the caves. It tells of hunts, beasts of the ice age, and art cut in bone and horn. The work is the first learned report on cave life in the stone age, and a base text.
stewart-tait-unseen-universe-1875:
Balfour Stewart and P. G. Tait were two Scots men of science of high rank. Their Unseen Universe came out in 1875 with no names on it at first. They argue that laws of heat and force point to a world past sight. That world, they hold, holds the soul's life to come.

Heat must run down, they grant, and the stars must cool in time. Yet force is never lost, they say, but flows to an unseen realm. Faith and lab facts meet in a bold, strange blend. The book was a hit and stirred years of talk on science and faith.
academy-resolution-1775:
In 1775 the Royal Academy of Sciences in Paris took a firm step. The school said it would no longer read plans for perpetual motion. Such plans claimed a wheel or mill that runs for all time with no fuel. The French text prints the full terms of the ban.

The school gives hard grounds for the step. Such schemes waste the funds of poor homes, it says, and yield no gain at all. Hope of a prize kept men at the vain hunt for years. The ban marks the point where top science shut the door on the dream.
heckethorn-secret-societies-1875:
Charles William Heckethorn cast a wide net in The Secret Societies of All Ages and Countries in 1875. No guild or cult of note slips past his sweep. The book starts with the rites of Egypt, Greece, and Rome. It runs on to the groups of his own Victorian day.

Knights Templar, Rosicrucians, and Freemasons take long runs of text. So do the Carbonari, the Mafia's kin, and odd cults of the East. Heckethorn tells of signs, oaths, and the ends each group sought. The book is a vast store house of tales on hid groups.
swedenborg-earths-in-the-universe-1875:
Emanuel Swedenborg first wrote of the earths in the sky in 1758. The dress here is the English one of 1875. Its full old title speaks of the earths in our solar scheme. Swedenborg said spirits from those worlds spoke with him for years.

Moon folk, Mars folk, and the rest pass in a long chain of tales. Each race has its own bent of mind and way of faith. Swedenborg links their traits to the parts of one grand man in heaven. The book is the root text of the faith view of peopled worlds.
emerson-letters-and-social-aims-1875:
Ralph Waldo Emerson published Letters and Social Aims in 1875, his final collection in his lifetime. The volume holds Poetry and Imagination, The Comic, Quotation and Originality, and Immortality among its essays in print. Emerson, aging and forgetful, had help from his children and friends in shaping this last book.

Poetry and Imagination restates his faith that metaphor is the mind's first and deepest native tongue in man. Quotation and Originality defends borrowing, since all minds are built from the thoughts of other minds before them. The Comic finds laughter a moral sense, and Immortality closes with serene trust beyond creed and proof in death. Persian Poetry and Social Aims show his range from Hafiz to the manners of American drawing rooms. The book is a gentle envoi to a forty-year career of American letters.
eddy-science-and-health-1875:
Mary Baker Eddy published Science and Health with Key to the Scriptures in 1875, after years of illness and Bible study. The book sets out her system of spiritual healing, in which disease is an error of mortal mind. It became the founding textbook of Christian Science.

Eddy argues that God is all, that matter and sickness have no true reality, and that right understanding heals the body. The closing section, the Key to the Scriptures, reads Genesis and Revelation as spiritual allegory rather than plain history. Her system built a worldwide church, with reading rooms and practitioners in many lands.
spurgeon-lectures-to-my-students-1875:
Spurgeon's Lectures to My Students, published in 1875, gather his Friday talks to the men of his Pastors' College in London. The college trained working men for the Baptist ministry without charging fees. The lectures cover preaching from call to delivery.

Spurgeon advises on voice, gesture, sermon choice, prayer, and the pastor's own temptations and sorrows. His wit is famous: whole pages read like stand-up comedy with a theological point underneath. Generations of preachers have called the book the wittiest work on homiletics, the art of preaching, ever written. Students treasured the talks enough to print them for a wider world.
darwin-insectivorous-plants-1875:
Charles Darwin published Insectivorous Plants in 1875, after years of experiments on plants that catch and digest insects. Sundews in his greenhouse at Down had caught his eye in 1860. He tested leaves with meat, insects, and chemicals to see how they moved and fed.

Darwin found that leaves of the sundew bend, secrete acid, and dissolve animal matter much like a stomach does. He tested many kinds, from Venus flytraps to butterworts, and mapped how each trap worked. The results stretched the line between plant and animal behavior. The book remains a landmark of plant study, built almost wholly on careful trials anyone could repeat at home.
moliere-dramatic-works-vanlaun-vol1-1875:
Henri van Laun translated the complete plays of Molière into English, and the first volume appeared in 1875. Molière, who died in 1673, was France's great writer of stage comedy. Volume one gathers his early plays, written before his fame was secure.

The volume holds The Blunderer, The Love-Tiff, and The Pretentious Young Ladies. It also holds Sganarelle and the serious verse play Don Garcia of Navarre. Readers can watch Molière learn his craft: quick plots, mistaken lovers, and servants who outwit their masters. Van Laun added notes on the French stage, and his set stayed the standard English Molière for decades.
moliere-dramatic-works-vanlaun-vol2-1875:
Volume two of Henri van Laun's English Molière came out in 1875, the same year as the first. By the plays in this volume, Molière ran his own company in Paris under royal favor. The centerpiece is The School for Wives, the hit that made him a major figure.

Alongside it stand The School for Husbands and the slight, witty piece called The Bores. Van Laun also prints Molière's own defense, The School for Wives Criticised, plus The Impromptu of Versailles. The Forced Marriage rounds out the volume. Together the plays show comedy turning sharper, as Molière began to mock manners, marriage, and pride in earnest.
moliere-dramatic-works-vanlaun-vol3-1875:
Two of Molière's greatest plays anchor volume three of the van Laun translation, issued in 1875. Don Juan retells the tale of the bold seducer who defies heaven itself. The Misanthrope gives Alceste, a man so wedded to truth that he ruins his own love and standing.

The volume also holds The Princess of Elis, a courtly entertainment with music. Love Is the Best Doctor offers a brisk farce on quack physicians. The Physician in Spite of Himself turns a woodcutter into a fake doctor by force. The mix shows Molière's full range, from deep character study to broad, fast farce.
indian-poetry-arnold-1875:
Edwin Arnold published Indian Poetry in 1875, gathering his verse renderings from Sanskrit sources. Its centerpiece, The Indian Song of Songs, was the first English verse translation of Jayadeva's Gita Govinda. That twelfth-century poem sings the love of Krishna and Radha in songs of great sweetness and daring.

Arnold adds two books from the Mahabharata, wise sayings from the Hitopadesa, and other Oriental poems. His light, musical English aimed to make India's classics sing for Victorian readers. Arnold later won wide fame with The Light of Asia, his life of the Buddha in verse. This earlier volume shows the same gift at work. The Gutenberg text is ebook 25965.
chanson-croisade-albigeoise-vol-1-1875:
The Chanson de la Croisade Albigeoise is a long poem in Old Provençal that tells the Albigensian Crusade as it happened, from 1209 onward. Two poets made it: a cleric who cheered the crusaders, and a second, nameless hand who took the side of Toulouse. Paul Meyer edited the text in 1875, and this is his first tome. The language is the tongue of the troubadours.

Sieges, burnings of heretics, the fall of Béziers and Carcassonne, and the death of kings crowd the verse. No other work lets readers hear the south of France speak of its own ruin. Meyer adds the apparatus of a modern edition to the old song. It is the crusade's great vernacular narrative.
allen-encyclopedia-pure-materia-medica-v:
In 1875 the third volume of Allen's Encyclopaedia of Pure Materia Medica took its place in the set. The design stays fixed: every known proving symptom, arranged by remedy, with nothing left out for neatness. Allen believed a prescriber should judge the record, not an editor's summary.

Long entries let patterns surface on their own, as the same odd sign recurs across provers. Short ones show how thin some drug records still were. Either way, the volume serves the working method of the school: match the patient's signs to the fullest drug picture available, then choose.

Allen's Encyclopaedia reached Volume IV in 1875, and the archive of provings kept growing steadily. Timothy Field Allen served as gatherer rather than judge, printing proving symptoms from journals, books, and private reports alike. Each remedy entry sorts its harvest by part of the body, in the set's fixed order.

The worth of the whole set lies in that restraint. Later writers could build keynotes and guiding symptoms on ground Allen had cleared, knowing the raw record sat behind them. Volume IV, mid-set, shows the scale of his ambition: ten full volumes to hold what the world's provers had seen.
childers-pali-dictionary-1875:
Robert Caesar Childers gave Pali studies their first dictionary in 1875, A Dictionary of the Pali Language, his life's work. Pali, the language of the oldest Buddhist canon, had few tools for English readers before his book appeared. Childers built entries from the texts themselves, with roots, forms, and citations drawn from scripture and commentary.

Every translator of the Pali canon since has stood on this groundwork, directly or through those it taught. The dictionary also spread knowledge of Buddhist terms and ideas far beyond the academy walls. Childers died young, in the year of publication, yet his single great book founded a field's daily practice in the West.
gitagovinda-arnold-1875:
Edwin Arnold sang Jayadeva's Gitagovinda in English in 1875 as The Indian Song of Songs, a rendering of love and faith. Jayadeva's twelfth-century Sanskrit lyric drama tells of Radha and Krishna: their longing, their parting, and their reunion in the spring woods. Songs meant for singing carry the lovers' moods, while Krishna's godhood shines through the human play of desire.

Hindu devotion cherishes the poem as scripture set to music, sung in temples and festivals to this day. Arnold, famed across the world for The Light of Asia, gave its erotic mysticism a lush Victorian voice. His rendering remains the best known English path into Jayadeva's masterpiece for new readers.
plos-pone-0003375:
Weizhong Li, John C. Wooley, and Adam Godzik faced a data problem in this 2008 paper. Ocean sampling trips had produced millions of protein sequences from sea water. Grouping near-matching sequences is a first step, but the sets were too large for old tools. The authors present a fast way to cluster very large sequence sets.

Their method sorts the huge ocean data into groups of like proteins. Grouping cuts the data down to a size that gene catalogs can handle. The paper shows the approach working on the full ocean sampling set. Faster grouping helps turn raw sea DNA into maps of what microbes do.
plos-pone-0003475:
Wonkuk Kim, Derek Gordon, and Jonathan Sebat tackled study design for DNA copy variants in this 2008 paper. Some DNA stretches appear in unlike copy counts between people. Those variants may shape disease risk and onset. At the time, finding them relied mainly on microarray tools.

Case-control studies need enough people to spot real links reliably. The authors computed power and sample size for such studies. Their method uses a likelihood ratio test built on mixture models. The worked examples show planners how large a study must be. Most gene hunts fail on power long before they fail on ideas.
plos-pone-0003575:
Hong-Hee Won, Hee-Jin Kim, and Kyung-A Lee catalogued human coding variants in this 2008 paper. Data on sequence variation in the human genome were growing fast. Predicting what each variant does to health was growing more urgent. The team focused on variations inside coding sequences.

Their catalog covered protein-coding changes stored in genome databases. It weighed predicted functional effects for each entry. Order in the data helps separate harmless variants from risky ones. Clinicians and gene hunters both rely on such inventories. Clinics already use such lists when they read a patient's genome report.
plos-pone-0003675:
Charlotte A. Oomen, Carlos E. N. Girardi, Rudy Cahyadi, and colleagues published this brain study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Depression strikes women more often than men, and early life stress may be one reason why. The team studied what removing rat pups from their mothers does to the developing brain.

They measured neurogenesis, the birth of new brain cells, in the hippocampus. Early maternal deprivation changed that growth in opposite directions in males and females. The split result offers a clue to why depression linked to early stress does not fall evenly on the two sexes.
plos-pone-0003775:
Chrisantha Fernando, K. K. Karishma, and Eörs Szathmáry published this theory paper in PLOS ONE in 2008. No model existed for how a neuronal network might copy its own wiring pattern. Such copying could matter for how brains draw conclusions and reuse learned functions. The authors propose a mechanism.

Their proposal copies the topology, the connection layout, of neuronal networks within the brain. They argue it could support causal inference, function copying, and even natural selection among ideas inside one head. The paper gives neuroscience a concrete model of learning by internal copying.
plos-pone-0003875:
Meredith E. Young, Geoffrey R. Norman, and Karin R. Humphreys studied how medical words shape public views in 2008. Their PLOS ONE article asks what happens when plain conditions gain formal medical names. One case they cite is impotence, now more often called erectile dysfunction. New names can change how serious, common, or treatable a condition seems.

The authors set out to test the effect of medical terms on how people judge illness. Their work treats language itself as part of health care, not just a label on it. The findings matter for doctors who choose words with patients. They also matter for public debate about newly named disorders.
plos-pone-0003975:
Maarten A. N. Rits, Karel A. van Dort, and Neeltje A. Kootstra studied gene variants and HIV risk in 2008. Cyclophilin A is a protein HIV uses during infection. Earlier studies tied variants near its gene to HIV susceptibility. They also tied them to how fast disease progresses.

Their PLOS ONE article tested those variants in a defined study group. The authors asked whether the variants affect catching HIV-1 itself. Control regions of genes can tune how much protein cells make. Confirming such effects helps explain why risk differs between people. The paper came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for work in science and health.
plos-pone-0004075:
W. Jason Cummings, David W. Bednarski, and Nancy Maizels studied how chemical tags on DNA affect variation in 2008. Homologous recombination repairs damaged genes using a matching donor. That repair is essential for keeping the genome intact. It must pick proper donors and avoid faulty ones.

Their PLOS ONE article reports epigenetic modification stimulates genetic variation. Tags that do not change DNA sequence altered recombination outcomes. Repair can copy small differences from the donor into the target. Such gene conversion quietly spreads variation through populations. The study ran in PLOS ONE, an open journal read by labs around the world.
plos-pone-0004175:
Achia Urbach and Nissim Benvenisty published this stem cell study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Turner syndrome, caused by having only one X chromosome, is one of the most common chromosome abnormalities in females. About three percent of pregnancies start as XO embryos, yet nearly all of them end during the first trimester.

The usual genetic explanation for this early loss was incomplete. Using human embryonic stem cells as a model, the authors studied why XO embryos so rarely survive. Their work aims at the hidden first weeks of pregnancy, where most of these embryos are lost before anyone knows they existed.
plos-pone-0004275:
Yujung Kang and colleagues published this imaging study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Measuring blood flow in peripheral tissue accurately is hard, yet it is necessary to diagnose poor circulation in limbs. Near-infrared light penetrates tissue relatively deeply, so fluorescence imaging with it has drawn much attention.

The team present a quantitative analysis of peripheral tissue perfusion using spatiotemporal molecular dynamics, tracking how tracer molecules move through tissue over space and time. The method was built for limbs, where poor flow does real harm. Their method aims to turn glowing pictures into numbers doctors can trust. Better flow numbers mean earlier detection of limbs at risk.
plos-pone-0004375:
Macquarie Island is a small subantarctic island south of New Zealand. Its rockhopper, royal, and king penguins often carry a seabird tick called Ixodes uriae. Lee Major, May La Linn, Robert Slade, and co-authors examined those ticks for viruses. Their 2009 PLOS ONE paper reports what they found living inside the ticks.

The team isolated viruses from four separate genera in the ticks. The set held a flavivirus, an orbivirus, a phlebovirus, and a nairovirus. All four groups include viruses spread by biting insects or ticks. The finding shows remote penguin colonies host a wide mix of viruses. It also gives disease trackers a baseline for this far southern outpost.
plos-pone-0004475: In 2009, Collins, Gnocchi, and White found twin genes running muscle repair. Integrated functions of Pax3 and Pax7 in muscle growth and differentiation were mapped. The paired factors steered satellite cells. The finding aids muscle therapy. The twins divide the labor.
plos-pone-0004575: In 2009, a team mapped immune gene assembly's starting gun. Initiation of V(D)J recombination by Dβ-associated recombination signal sequences was dissected. The two-step process obeyed a strict constraint. The neat finding maps immunity's deep origins. The tight control is critical.
plos-pone-0004675: In 2009, Cheon, Wang, and Deng found a famous cancer marker expendable in mice anew. CA125/MUC16 proved dispensable for mouse development and reproduction. The knockout mice thrived normally. The finding reframes the biomarker story. The blood marker tracks ovarian cancer.
plos-pone-0004775: In 2009, a team linked a repair protein's signal to its gene's state anew. Even MGMT staining matched a clean MGMT gene switch in brain tumors. The staining told the gene's state. The study guides brain-tumor care. The test marker is telling.
zola-abbe-mouret-1875:
Vizetelly's opening essay places Abbe Mouret's Transgression with care in the saga. Issued fourth, it stands ninth in Zola's final plan for the set. It grows out of The Conquest of Plassans and its wrecked Mouret home.

Serge Mouret, seen as a child there, now serves as priest of Les Artaud. That near-pagan hamlet sits in bare, burning country in Provence. Illness strands him in the wild walled garden of Le Paradou. There he loves the free Albine, and nature wars with the Church in him. Lush and sad, the tale holds one of the finest love stories in the cycle.
olive-branch-petition-1775:
The Continental Congress sent the Olive Branch Petition to the king in 1775. Shots had been fired, yet Congress still pleads for peace. The text stands as the colonies' last bid for reconciliation.

The delegates swear loyalty, list their wrongs, and beg for redress. They blame grasping ministers, not the king, for the growing crisis. George III refuses to read the plea and brands them rebels. With that door shut, the road to independence lies open. The petition's failure taught moderates that no middle path remained at all. John Dickinson drafted it hoping reason could still stop a war.
declaration-causes-necessity-1775:
Congress issued its Declaration of Taking Up Arms in 1775. The full title speaks of the Causes and Necessity of that step. A year before independence, the colonies explain why they fight.

We have counted the cost, the text declares in famed words. Nothing, it says, is so dreadful as voluntary slavery to power. The delegates deny any wish to break from Britain just yet. They blame Parliament's taxes and troops for forcing arms into hands. The Revolution's manifesto sets terms that independence soon outgrew within a year. Its slavery line still echoes through the founding era's debates.
treaty-of-orleans-1275:
The Treaty of Orléans of 1275 joins England and France in this record. The pact belongs to the reign of Edward I of England. Medieval kings settle their cross-Channel claims in formal, sworn terms.

Homage is rendered, disputes are compromised, and peace is sworn. Two great crowns of Christendom compose their quarrel for a season. The forms are solemn: seals, oaths, and kinship ties bind the deal. Thirteenth-century statecraft shows its formal face in the treaty's clauses. Short truces like this one paved the road to longer wars between the crowns. The record's sparse detail leaves the pact's exact terms to the clauses themselves.
helsinki-final-act-1975:
Thirty-five nations signed the Helsinki Final Act in Finland in 1975, closing a long conference on security in Europe. The United States, Canada, the Soviet Union, and nearly all European states took part. The act was not a treaty, but a set of political promises meant to ease Cold War tensions.

The West accepted Europe's postwar borders as settled, which Moscow had long wanted. In return, the Soviet bloc promised to respect human rights, free movement, and the flow of information. Dissidents across Eastern Europe seized on those promises, forming Helsinki watch groups that pressed their governments to keep them. Historians credit that pressure with helping to loosen the Soviet grip and end the Cold War.
cairnes-character-logical-method-1875:
John Elliott Cairnes published The Character and Logical Method of Political Economy in 1875. Cairnes, an Irish economist, was the friend and heir of John Stuart Mill. His book asks a basic question: what kind of science is economics, and how should it reason?

Cairnes defends the deductive method, which starts from known facts about human motives and argues toward conclusions. He answers the German historical school, which wanted economics rebuilt from case studies alone. The book also fixes the limits of the science, separating what economics can settle from what belongs to politics or morals. Clear and firm, it became the classic statement of classical method, read wherever economists argued about how their subject should work.
jevons-money-mechanism-exchange-1875:
Jevons published Money and the Mechanism of Exchange in 1875, a short classic on what money is and how it works. He wrote it for general readers as much as for students, in the clear style that marked his best work. At the time, banking crises and currency debates made the subject urgent on both sides of the Atlantic.

The book explains why barter fails, what makes a good currency material, and how coins, notes, and cheques each do money's work. Jevons treats the standard of value, minting, and paper money with calm precision. Generations of students learned the subject from these chapters. The primer is still quoted for its clarity, and historians count it the clearest short book on money in English. It shows a founder of modern economics writing at the height of his powers.
maine-lectures-early-history-institution:
Maine's Lectures on the Early History of Institutions appeared in 1875, a sequel in spirit to his famous Ancient Law. Maine taught that modern institutions could only be understood by tracing them to their primitive forms. The lectures range widely, drawing on his years in India and on the old laws of Ireland.

He treats kingship, property, and the family in their earliest shapes, comparing the Brehon laws of Ireland with the customs of India and Rome. The comparative method is the star: distant societies are set side by side to reveal a common pattern of growth. Maine writes with the confidence of a man opening a new science. The book was the comparative method's masterpiece in legal history, and later scholars have argued with it ever since, which is its own kind of tribute.
cia-0000008775:
One week in South Vietnam, April 8 to 14, 1965, fills a CIA situation report on military and political affairs. American Marines had landed at Da Nang the month before, and bombing of the north was under way. Saigon's government, meanwhile, kept changing hands.

Weekly reports stitched battlefield news to the capital's unstable politics in a single judgment. Policymakers used them to track whether the war effort was gaining or slipping. This week's entry catches the conflict at its great turning point, when American ground war began. Reading it now shows escalation judged day by day, not in hindsight.
cia-0000009975:
An American prisoner of war was sighted in Tay Ninh province, South Vietnam, a report dated January 1973 states. Tay Ninh, northwest of Saigon against the Cambodian border, had been a Viet Cong stronghold all war long. The date places the sighting in the ceasefire month itself.

A prisoner seen in the border province as peace began posed the usual hard alternatives. He might be awaiting release, hidden, or misreported altogether. The report entered the postwar files where such questions lived for years. This entry preserves the Tay Ninh claim at the moment the war's fighting formally stopped.
cia-0000010475:
Key problems facing American efforts to strengthen the Near East are listed in a March 1951 CIA paper. The Near East of the title runs from Egypt toward Pakistan in the usage of the time. Washington wanted a friendly barrier along the Soviet Union's southern edge.

The paper names the obstacles plainly: nationalism, weak states, Arab-Israeli conflict, and oil politics. Such candor helps readers see why the grand design kept failing. Alliance schemes drawn in Washington met a region pushing the other way. This early file states the mismatch at the start of a decade of trying.
cia-0000012275:
What a spy sends must be listed. An undated CIA document, its year estimated as 1961, inventories materials and documents to be sent in the Penkovsky case. The manifest belongs to the working file of the operation that ran Oleg Penkovsky, the Soviet colonel whose product filled whole shelves. Lists like this one kept track of a haul too valuable to handle loosely.

The inventory names the pieces of the colonel's product and the papers that moved with them. It shows clerks accounting for secrets with the care of bankers counting cash. For readers, the list is the case file's own catalog of its treasures.
cia-0000012375:
Joseph J. Bulik wrote to the chief of the Soviet Russia division in April 1963 about Oleg Penkovsky, and the memo opens the case's internal reckoning.
